newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude, products futures break to upside.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude, products futures break to upside.

text.p: NYMEX crude and oil products futures moved up sharply on Monday as crude broke through a key technical resistance level and broke out of a range holding it in for a month, traders said.
The move was partly initiated by market supportive news over the weekend, including tension in the Middle East, traders added.
June light crude futures on NYMEX, were up 91 cents at $21.34 a barrel just before 1300 EDT/1700 GMT.
"This is what technical traders live and die for," said Hans Kashyap, an analyst at Analytics Research Corp in Maryland.

Crude futures formed "a perfect bottom," hitting $18.96 twice in early April, Kashyap said. Since then the $20.50/55 area has been tested a number of times, an area where a lot of stop-loss 'buy' orders were placed by short-coverers and those playing the long side.

The breakout came during out-of-hours trading on the ACCESS system early Monday and meant there was a gap at the open of $20.52 (Friday's close at $20.43), giving the market some strong early momentum.
Signals suggest crude should test up to $21.80 later Monday, techincal traders said.

Products futures were in even more bullish shape. June heating oil was up 1.73 cents at 56.25 a gallon, while gasoline was 1.63 higher at 64.50. Both had about a cent to go before encountering main resistance levels.
Though there was no news of serious disruption, there was enough potentially disruptive news to give the market a boost to move through technical targets, analysts said.
Two major crude oil suppliers, Iran and Colombia, suffered earthquakes over the weekend, though there was no news of actual damage to oil production.
Tension in the Middle East was raised as a U.S. military commander pledged to protect the Strait of Hormuz amid the launch of new wargames by Iran in the Middle East Gulf.
Also, an Iraqi opposition organization said Baghdad troops were amassing in the north of the country, though Washington administration spokespeople downplayed the reports.

Meanwhile, loadings at the key Sullom Voe port in Scotland's Shetland Islands, the port which loads Brent blend crude, were temporarily halted as protesting fishermen blocked its entrance. The disruption was not expected to last, however, according to North Sea crude traders.

"We saw the same Iranian war games a month ago," said Nizam Sharif, an analyst at Hornsby & Co in Houston. He said the news from Iran last week was also of oversupply by OPEC, when several of the seven OPEC ministers met for an oil conference in central Iran complained of quota-busting by other members.
